transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 16:30 PT
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Narang (Redwood SE), Evan Cross (Paladin, Head of ML), Maya Liu (Paladin, Infra Lead), Samir Patel (Paladin, VP Eng)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on cost/unit economics for potential Redwood deployment. Paladin is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for a multi-model inference workload. Key asks: per-token and per-embedding economics, batching and caching levers, budget guardrails, and pilot scope to validate unit cost claims.

Topics:
- Current stack and traffic profile
- Per-token pricing and how batching/caching affect unit costs
- Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs (cost, latency, data residency)
- Benchmarking approach and pilot plan
- Security/compliance docs request

Action items (recap in call): see metadata action_items list

Transcript:
00:00 Jordan: hey everybody, this is Jordan from Redwood, thanks for carving out time today. we have Priya here who'll cover some of the technical bits, and we'll focus on cost and how we can hit Paladin's constraints.
00:06 Evan: great, thanks Jordan. um, quick context, we're a quant research org, so model throughput and predictable unit cost is like, top priority. we run multiple transformer models for scoring and reranking across our pipelines.
00:18 Maya: yeah hi, i'm maya, i run infra, so my thing is ensuring we don't blow budget on inference. we have spikes during market opens and need to cap monthly spend.
00:27 Priya: awesome, thanks. i'll try to walk through typical levers — per-token pricing, batching, prefix/kv caching, and Dedicated options — and then we can map that to your traffic.
00:36 Samir: quick one, do you have an initial sense of hosted per-token vs reserved (dedicated) unit costs? like ballpark?
00:44 Jordan: sure. ballpark — hosted API is our fastest onramp, per-token model depending, but for gen models expect 0.6 to 3.5 cents per 1k tokens for small-medium family, big LLMs higher. for enterprise scale or reserved capacity, unit costs can drop substantially because of amortized GPU utilization, often 30-60% lower per-token relative to on-demand. i'll send the exact sheet after.
01:10 Evan: ok, sounds like a big range. what moves it most, is it just GPU type or is it batching and kv cache?
01:18 Priya: it's all of the above. primary drivers: model family and size, GPU/quantization profile, batching efficiency, and cache hit rates. for example if you have high prefix reuse across requests our KV cache can serve repeated prefixes without regenerating tokens, that can drop effective per-token cost dramatically.
01:35 Maya: when you say 'kv cache' are you referring to the per-session KV cache or some prefix cache? we've got a lot of repeated prompts for daily signals.
01:43 Priya: both. we have short-lived session KV for streaming, plus prefix caching for common prompts. sometimes the auto-prefix cache is mis-transcribed in notes as 'K-V cash' so sorry if that's in the docs, but it basically avoids re-computing attention for the same token prefixes.
02:00 Evan: makes sense. can you quantify — say we have 1M inference calls per day, average input 120 tokens, output 80 tokens, and maybe 40% prefix reuse. what would a hosted vs dedicated estimate look like?
02:14 Jordan: rough mental math — 1M calls * 200 tokens = 200M tokens/day. at 30 days = 6B tokens. with hosted at say $0.002 per 1k tokens (example) that's about $12K/month; but that's a simplistic number and model selection changes it. with dedicated, if you can pack workloads and get batching/k-v reuse you might get down to $5-8K equivalent for the same effective output. we'll run this in the spreadsheet with your exact numbers.
02:45 Samir: ok but our worry is tail latency during spikes. dedicated gives guaranteed capacity, right?
02:51 Priya: yes dedicated is reserved GPU pools, predictable throughput. we also offer burst capacity and autoscale policies, but the main tradeoff is you commit to reserved compute (monthly). dedicated delivers lower per-call variance and better unit economics if you sustain enough utilization.
03:06 Maya: what about private deployment (VPC/on-prem)? our compliance folks prefer customer-managed infra, but that'll change costs.
03:13 Jordan: private deployments add infra overhead and support/licensing. unit costs depend on your hardware, but Redwood can provide private control plane and our runtime; you get full data residency but you'll need to provision GPU fleet and we help with kernel selection and quantization guidance. for some customers the total TCO is higher but acceptable for compliance reasons.
03:31 Evan: what's the minimal pilot you recommend to validate the unit economics claims? we want something 4 weeks-ish to measure cost/per-token and latency under realistic load.
03:39 Priya: our typical pilot is 3-4 weeks: 1 week onboarding (credentials, sample traffic, quickstart), 2 weeks of benchmarks at your traffic profile, 1 week of analysis and tuning. we instrument batching thresholds, cache configs, model variants, and record per-token telemetry.
03:55 Jordan: we can also run an A/B compare against your current provider (if you want) to show delta in unit cost and latency. that usually helps procurement.
04:05 Maya: how invasive is the instrumentation? we prefer not to route traffic through a third-party long-term. can benchmarks be run from mirror traffic?
04:12 Priya: yes mirror traffic is standard and recommended for cost-sensitive benchmarks. we take sample logs and replay locally into a test fleet, or use a short-lived proxy in your VPC for a closed pilot.
04:23 Evan: you mentioned batching efficiency; what's the knob there? do you recommend aggressive batching always?
04:28 Priya: there's a latency vs throughput trade. Redwood's runtime supports adaptive batching and dynamic batch size based on latency SLOs. for background scoring you can batch aggressively to maximize GPU utilization; for low-latency front-end calls we set small max batch sizes and rely more on caching. the optimizer suggests batching params based on your sequence length distribution.
04:50 Samir: and do you charge per-second GPU or is it abstracted into per-token billing for hosted?
04:55 Jordan: hosted is per-token for gen/embeddings with included infra. for dedicated we have reserved capacity pricing (monthly invoice) and then a unit economics calculator that maps to effective per-token cost given utilization. private deployments are licensed and then you cover infra.
05:10 Maya: any discounts or committed-use tiers?
05:13 Jordan: yes committed reserved capacity discounts are typical — multi-month commitments reduce unit price. volume tiers in hosted also reduce per-token price. we'll include both in the sheet.
05:24 Evan: regarding caching, how do you enforce data retention and privacy when using prefix cache in hosted mode?
05:31 Priya: good question. hosted offers configurable retention policies and encryption at rest; we can scope the cache to not store sensitive inputs, or use per-customer KMS for encryption. for most sensitive use cases we recommend Dedicated or Private with customer-managed keys.
05:47 Samir: we need SOC 2 and network diagrams before we can go deeper.
05:50 Jordan: we'll send SOC 2, SOC 2 type II cert details, and a network architecture doc. noted.
05:55 Maya: what about multi-model routing? we run ensembles and sometimes route to smaller models for cheap passes. can that be automated for cost savings?
06:04 Priya: yes, Redwood supports smart routing policies: route by latency, cost, model family, and fallback. you can do a cheap filter model first and then route to a larger model only when needed. that saves unit cost significantly.
06:18 Evan: what's the expected overhead of that routing in terms of latency?
06:21 Priya: negligible if the first pass is small; the overhead is the extra network hop, but you avoid a full forward on the big model most of the time so it pays off.
06:30 Jordan: to ground this, we'll run a quick back-of-envelope with your numbers and include a sensitivity table: varying cache hit rate (0%, 25%, 50%) and batching effectiveness.
06:40 Evan: great. one more question — do you offer tokenized pricing for embedding calls differently? embeddings are cheap but heavy volume for us.
06:48 Jordan: embeddings are priced differently — usually per-embedding unit with volume tiers. we'll break that out in the pricing sheet.
06:55 Samir: how often do you see customers realize the 30-60% reduction you mentioned when moving to dedicated?
06:59 Priya: most customers with steady-state, predictable load who accept some commit see 30-50% unit savings after tuning batching and quantization. if you can use higher batch sizes and leverage prefix reuse it's closer to 50-60% in some cases.
07:14 Maya: any pitfalls? e.g., customers over-commit and then underutilize.
07:18 Jordan: yep that's the main pitfall. we'll simulate utilization curves in the spreadsheet and offer autoscale and burst policies to reduce risk; for some customers we recommend a hybrid — reserved for baseline and hosted bursts for peaks.
07:31 Evan: pricing transparency is important to us. we want a clear model with tokens in, tokens out, and overheads.
07:37 Jordan: agreed. we'll provide a detailed calculator that shows per-token math, per-hour GPU amortization, and impact of cache/hit rates.
07:46 Maya: can Priya run a quick example of how batching helps? like with a toy sequence length distribution?
07:50 Priya: sure — imagine 100 requests with average sequence 100 tokens. If you batch 16 you'll fill GPU more efficiently; with our runtime optimized kernels and quantization you reduce per-token GPU cycles. in practice the gain depends on variance; high variance reduces batching efficiency.
08:12 Evan: are there any hidden costs — e.g., data transfer, logging, observability retention?
08:17 Jordan: we charge for extended observability retention and some add-ons; basic tracing and token-level cost breakdown is included but long-term retention and audit exports can be add-ons. we'll call those out.
08:29 Samir: ok good. on procurement side we'll need a proposal showing pilot costs and expected ROI.
08:34 Jordan: we'll draft a pilot proposal that includes a not-to-exceed cap so you control spend during the pilot.
08:40 Maya: for the pilot, we'll share a traffic sample and define a small set of endpoints to exercise. who on your side will own the bench run?
08:46 Priya: i'll own the bench run with assistance from Jordan for access and account setup.
08:51 Evan: timeline wise we wanna start mid-march if possible.
08:54 Jordan: that's doable. we'll target onboarding the week of Mar 9 and run the 3-week benchmark after that.
08:59 Maya: one last technical — quantization: do you support int8/4 and how does that impact quality?
09:04 Priya: yes we support int8 and int4 quant profiles; usually 8-bit is a safe sweet spot for many models with minimal quality degradation. our Optimize team runs evaluation harnesses to ensure regressions are within your thresholds.
09:19 Evan: perfect. ok i think that's it for questions.
09:22 Jordan: recap quick: we'll send pricing sheet + calculator, SOC2 and network doc, bench scripts and quickstart repo, propose pilot plan and schedule a technical deep-dive with your infra team week of Mar 9.
09:35 Samir: thanks everyone. looking forward to the materials.
09:38 Maya: thanks.
09:39 Priya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email.
